newsitem.title: USA: Eagle-Picher urges speedy germanium stockpile sale.
newsitem.headline: Eagle-Picher urges speedy germanium stockpile sale.

text.p: Eagle-Picher Industries, the U.S. germanium producer, said the U.S. government should speed up its sale of surplus germanium to help plug the supply gap, and keep prices from staying too high which has encouraged substitution.
"I think the stockpile should sell 10 tonnes a year for four years rather than 4 tonnes a year for ten years," Dennis Thomas, Eagle-Picher's general manager told Reuters.
Thomas was attending a meeting here called by the Defense National Stockpile Center to discuss the U.S. government's first sale of germanium in several years.
Any change to the amount up for sale would have to be approved by the Congressional market impact committee, Connelly said.

For 1997 Thomas forecast global output of 75 tonnes of fresh production, and 30 tonnes of recycled metal, the latter a 50 percent increase on 1996. "This year total demand will probably be 125 tonnes," he added.
The gap in supply will have to be plugged by stockpiles.

Thomas estimated that last year some 5 to 8 tonnes of market share was lost as high metal prices prompted consumers to use rival materials, especially in applications such as PET plastics used in packaging, and positron emission tomography equipment in CAT scans.
Eagle-Picher wanted to see more stockpile material offloaded in the near-term to bridge the gap until more metal from elsewhere comes on stream in the coming years.
"I would say 50 percent of the germanium used in the world could be recycled," Thomas said.
Eagle-Picher's second biggest customer who deals in fiber optics, has never recycled metal but will begin doing so this year, reducing their offtake of virgin production.

Nevertheless the expectation of stockpile sales has begun to dampen prices, Thomas said. In January the Ukraine announced it sold some 4 tonnes of germanium, and Thomas believed this was the end of the Ukrainian stockpile.
"My understanding is there is 8.5 tonnes of metal left in the Russian stockpile and 29 tonnes of germanium dioxide, but I don't know how much of it is going to move," Thomas said.

He also noted that Japan, which bought more than 50 percent of its annual requirements in one application in 1995 were largely out of the market last year. "They could be serious buyers in 1997. There is potential demand from them and they could be bidding for the germanium oxide from Russia."
